title: Manual 4: Deploying Interactive Web Apps & Dashboards on CESNET Kubernetes
text:
Beyond batch scripts, our CESNET Kubernetes namespace (stenc-ns) can host live, 24/7 web applications—such as image review/annotation portals (e.g., RhizoPic Review, Fly Review), data dashboards, or R Shiny / Python Streamlit apps—with automatic Let’s Encrypt HTTPS certificates under the domain:
https://<your-app-name>-stenc.dyn.cloud.e-infra.cz

title: Manual 4: Deploying Interactive Web Apps & Dashboards on CESNET Kubernetes
section: 1. How Web Hosting Works on CESNET K8s
text:
1. How Web Hosting Works on CESNET K8s
Whereas a batch script uses a Job (which runs once and exits), a web application uses three Kubernetes objects defined together in templates/k8s/web-app-deployment.yaml:

Deployment: Runs your web server container (Flask/Waitress, FastAPI/Uvicorn, Streamlit, or Shiny) continuously on port 8080. If the container ever crashes or a cluster node reboots, Kubernetes automatically restarts it.
Service: Creates a stable internal network address inside stenc-ns forwarding port 80 to your container’s port 8080.
Ingress: Connects the public domain https://<your-app-name>-stenc.dyn.cloud.e-infra.cz to your Service and automatically provisions a free Let’s Encrypt SSL/TLS certificate via cert-manager.

Internet Browser (https://my-webapp-stenc.dyn.cloud.e-infra.cz)
       |
       v  (HTTPS / TLS handled automatically by cert-manager)
+--------------+
|   Ingress    |  (ingressClassName: nginx)
+------+-------+
       |
       v
+--------------+
|   Service    |  (Port 80 ---> TargetPort 8080)
+------+-------+
       |
       v
+--------------+      Reads & writes images/data      +---------------------+
|  Deployment  | <----------------------------------> | CESNET S3           |
|  (Pod: 8080) |      via s3-credentials Secret       | (peg-bucket)        |
+--------------+                                      +---------------------+

title: Manual 4: Deploying Interactive Web Apps & Dashboards on CESNET Kubernetes
section: 2. Step-by-Step: Deploying a Web App
text:
2. Step-by-Step: Deploying a Web App

Step 1: Prepare Your Application Files
For a lightweight Python web app (e.g., app.py and index.html), you don’t even need a custom Docker image—you can store the source files in a ConfigMap and stream heavy images/data directly from peg-bucket via boto3!
Minimal app.py example (listening on port 8080 with a /healthz endpoint for Kubernetes readiness checks):
# app.py
from flask import Flask, jsonify

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route("/healthz")
def healthz():
    return jsonify({"status": "ok"}), 200

@app.route("/")
def index():
    return "<h1>Hello from CESNET Kubernetes!</h1>"


Step 2: Upload Your Source Code into a ConfigMap
kubectl create configmap my-webapp-src -n stenc-ns \
  --from-file=app.py=app.py \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
(If you also have an index.html or helper scripts, simply add --from-file=index.html=index.html to the command above.)


Step 3: Configure and Apply web-app-deployment.yaml

Copy templates/k8s/web-app-deployment.yaml to your project folder.
Replace my-webapp with your app’s name (e.g., pollen-viewer), and set the Ingress host to <your-app-name>-stenc.dyn.cloud.e-infra.cz.
Apply the manifest:
kubectl apply -f web-app-deployment.yaml
Wait for the pod to become ready:
kubectl rollout status deployment/my-webapp -n stenc-ns

Within 30–60 seconds, cert-manager will issue the HTTPS certificate and your app will be live at https://<your-app-name>-stenc.dyn.cloud.e-infra.cz!

title: Manual 4: Deploying Interactive Web Apps & Dashboards on CESNET Kubernetes
section: 3. Updating a Live Web App (Zero Downtime)
text:
3. Updating a Live Web App (Zero Downtime)
Whenever you edit app.py or index.html, run these two commands to update the ConfigMap and perform a rolling restart of the deployment:
# 1. Update ConfigMap with the modified files
kubectl create configmap my-webapp-src -n stenc-ns \
  --from-file=app.py=app.py \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -

# 2. Trigger a rolling restart so the pod loads the new ConfigMap
kubectl rollout restart deployment/my-webapp -n stenc-ns
kubectl rollout status deployment/my-webapp -n stenc-ns

title: Manual 4: Deploying Interactive Web Apps & Dashboards on CESNET Kubernetes
section: 4. Deploying Streamlit or R Shiny Apps
text:
4. Deploying Streamlit or R Shiny Apps
You can use the exact same templates/k8s/web-app-deployment.yaml structure for Streamlit or R Shiny by changing only the image: and command: fields:

Option A: Streamlit App (app.py)
        image: python:3.12-slim
        command:
        - sh
        - -c
        - |
          pip install --user --quiet --no-warn-script-location streamlit boto3 pandas plotly
          /tmp/.local/bin/streamlit run /app/app.py \
            --server.port=8080 \
            --server.address=0.0.0.0 \
            --server.headless=true


Option B: R Shiny App (app.R)
        image: rocker/shiny:4.4.1
        command:
        - sh
        - -c
        - |
          mkdir -p /tmp/R_libs
          export HOME=/tmp R_LIBS_USER=/tmp/R_libs
          Rscript -e '
            if (!requireNamespace("aws.s3", quietly=TRUE)) {
              install.packages("aws.s3", repos="https://cloud.r-project.org", lib=Sys.getenv("R_LIBS_USER"))
            }
            shiny::runApp("/app/app.R", host="0.0.0.0", port=8080)
          '

title: Manual 4: Deploying Interactive Web Apps & Dashboards on CESNET Kubernetes
section: 5. Security Best Practices for Public Web Apps
text:
5. Security Best Practices for Public Web Apps
Because *.dyn.cloud.e-infra.cz URLs are reachable from the internet:

Always require login credentials if your web app can modify data, save annotations back to S3, or display unpublished datasets. Store user passwords/tokens in a Kubernetes Secret (never hardcoded in ConfigMap or Git), just like our rhizo-review-users secret:
kubectl create secret generic my-webapp-users -n stenc-ns \
  --from-file=users.json=users.json \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
Never expose your S3 keys to the browser frontend: Keep all boto3 / aws.s3 calls inside the backend Python/R server, or proxy S3 image streams through your backend endpoints.

title: Manual 2: Getting Started with CESNET Kubernetes (e-INFRA CZ / CERIT-SC)
text:
Our group uses the CERIT-SC / e-INFRA CZ Kubernetes platform (rancher.cloud.e-infra.cz) to run compute-intensive R and Python scripts, train deep-learning models on NVIDIA GPUs, and host interactive web applications.
This manual walks you through:

title: Manual 2: Getting Started with CESNET Kubernetes (e-INFRA CZ / CERIT-SC)
section: 1. Getting Access to e-INFRA CZ & Rancher
text:
1. Getting Access to e-INFRA CZ & Rancher

Step 1: Ensure You Have an Active e-INFRA CZ / MetaCentrum Account

All academic staff and students at Czech universities (Charles University, CAS, etc.) can register for free at e-infra.cz.
To access the Kubernetes cluster (kuba-cluster) and our shared project namespace (stenc-ns), ask Jakub to add your e-INFRA CZ / Perun username to the project namespace if you don’t see it yet.



Step 2: Log into the Rancher Web UI

Open your browser and go to: https://rancher.cloud.e-infra.cz
Click Log in with Shibboleth / e-INFRA CZ and sign in using your institutional login (e.g., Charles University CAS / eduID.cz).
In the Rancher home dashboard, click on the cluster kuba-cluster.
In the top namespace filter bar, select stenc-ns so you only view our group’s Pods, Jobs, Deployments, ConfigMaps, and Secrets.

title: Manual 2: Getting Started with CESNET Kubernetes (e-INFRA CZ / CERIT-SC)
section: 2. Setting Up kubectl on Your Computer
text:
2. Setting Up kubectl on Your Computer
While you can view logs and pods in the Rancher web browser, submitting scripts and streaming logs is much faster from your terminal using kubectl.

Step 1: Install kubectl

Linux (Ubuntu / Debian):
curl -LO "https://dl.k8s.io/release/$(curl -L -s https://dl.k8s.io/release/stable.txt)/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl"
chmod +x kubectl
sudo mv kubectl /usr/local/bin/
macOS (Homebrew):
brew install kubectl
Windows (PowerShell / Winget):
winget install -e --id Kubernetes.kubectl



Step 2: Download kubeconfig.yaml from Rancher

In the Rancher web UI (https://rancher.cloud.e-infra.cz), open kuba-cluster.
In the top-right corner of the screen, click the Document icon (“Download KubeConfig”).
Save the downloaded file as ~/.kube/config (Linux/macOS) or C:\Users\<YourUser>\.kube\config (Windows):
mkdir -p ~/.kube
mv ~/Downloads/kuba-cluster.yaml ~/.kube/config
chmod 600 ~/.kube/config
(Alternatively, if you keep kubeconfig.yaml inside a project folder, pass --kubeconfig kubeconfig.yaml or run export KUBECONFIG=/path/to/kubeconfig.yaml.)



Step 3: Set Your Default Namespace to stenc-ns and Test Connection
Run this one-liner so you don’t have to type -n stenc-ns on every single command:
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=stenc-ns
Now test your connection:
kubectl get pods -n stenc-ns
If you see a list of running/completed pods (or No resources found in stenc-ns namespace), your connection is working!






Tip



Troubleshooting error: You must be logged in to the server (Unauthorized): For security, Rancher API tokens inside kubeconfig.yaml expire periodically (every 30–90 days). Whenever you see Unauthorized, simply log into https://rancher.cloud.e-infra.cz, click Download KubeConfig again, and replace ~/.kube/config.

title: Manual 2: Getting Started with CESNET Kubernetes (e-INFRA CZ / CERIT-SC)
section: 3. Mandatory CERIT-SC Security Rules (Read Before Creating Pods!)
text:
3. Mandatory CERIT-SC Security Rules (Read Before Creating Pods!)
CERIT-SC enforces strict Pod Security Standards (restricted) to protect the shared university infrastructure. If you copy a generic Kubernetes YAML example from the internet, the cluster will reject it immediately unless it includes the following four settings:

Rule 1: Must Run as a Non-Root User (UID 1000)
Containers are forbidden from running as root (UID 0). Every Pod spec must include this securityContext at the Pod level (spec.template.spec.securityContext):
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 1000
        runAsGroup: 1000
        seccompProfile:
          type: RuntimeDefault


Rule 2: Must Drop Linux Capabilities & Privilege Escalation
Every container inside containers: must include this securityContext at the Container level:
        securityContext:
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          capabilities:
            drop:
            - ALL


Rule 3: Must Mount a Writable /app or /tmp Directory (emptyDir)
Because your container runs as user 1000 (not root), it cannot write files to / or /root and cannot install packages globally (pip install or install.packages() into /usr/local/lib will fail with Permission denied). To solve this cleanly:

Mount an emptyDir: {} volume at /app.
Set HOME=/app (and R_LIBS_USER=/app/R_libs for R, or pip install --user with PATH=/app/.local/bin:$PATH for Python).
All our templates in templates/k8s/ already configure this automatically!



Rule 4: Always Specify Resource requests and limits
Every container should state how much CPU, RAM (memory), and optionally GPU (nvidia.com/gpu) it needs:
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "4"
            memory: "8Gi"
          limits:
            cpu: "8"
            memory: "16Gi"

Important: If your R or Python script uses more RAM than limits.memory, Kubernetes will terminate the container immediately with status OOMKilled (Exit Code 137). If that happens, increase memory in your YAML (e.g., from 16Gi to 32Gi).

title: Manual 2: Getting Started with CESNET Kubernetes (e-INFRA CZ / CERIT-SC)
section: 4. Namespace Resource Quotas & CERIT-SC Limits
text:
4. Namespace Resource Quotas & CERIT-SC Limits
Every namespace on CERIT-SC Kubernetes has a total resource quota (ResourceQuota) shared across all currently running Pods in that namespace (Completed/Succeeded jobs do not consume quota):









Resource
Personal Namespace Quota (stenc-ns / <user>-ns)
Group Project Quota (on request via k8s@cerit-sc.cz)
Description




requests.cpu
20 CPU cores
12–64+ CPU cores
Guaranteed CPU cores reserved across all running pods


limits.cpu
32 CPU cores
64+ CPU cores
Maximum burst CPU ceiling across all running pods


requests.memory
40 GiB RAM
40–256+ GiB RAM
Guaranteed RAM reserved across all running pods


limits.memory
64 GiB RAM
256+ GiB RAM
Maximum RAM ceiling across all running pods (includes /dev/shm memory volumes)


nvidia.com/gpu
Uncapped in quota (limited by CPU/RAM quota)
Uncapped in quota
Multiple GPUs can run concurrently as long as pod CPU/RAM fits in the quota


Default per container
1 CPU / 512 MiB
1 CPU / 512 MiB
Applied automatically by LimitRange if resources: is omitted




Important Quota Tips for Colleagues:

Check Available Quota Before Submitting Large Jobs:
kubectl describe resourcequota -n stenc-ns
If limits.cpu or limits.memory is near 100%, a new job will wait until running jobs finish.
Use Your Own Personal Namespace (<username>-ns) for Extra Capacity: When you log into https://rancher.cloud.e-infra.cz, CERIT-SC automatically creates your own personal namespace (<surname>-ns) with its own independent 20/32 CPU and 40/64 GiB RAM quota! You can copy the s3-credentials Secret into your personal namespace and run jobs using your own quota while still reading and writing data to our shared peg-bucket S3 storage.
Idle GPU Pruning Policy: Interactive pods/notebooks requesting a GPU with < 0.005 (0.5%) GPU utilization for 2 consecutive days are automatically terminated by CERIT-SC so GPUs are not locked while idle. Always use kind: Job for GPU training so the GPU is released as soon as your script finishes.

title: Manual 2: Getting Started with CESNET Kubernetes (e-INFRA CZ / CERIT-SC)
section: 5. Essential kubectl Cheat Sheet
text:
5. Essential kubectl Cheat Sheet
All commands below assume you are working in namespace stenc-ns:







What You Want to Do
Command




List all pods and their status
kubectl get pods -n stenc-ns


List all batch jobs
kubectl get jobs -n stenc-ns


Submit / start a Job or Deployment
kubectl apply -f my-job.yaml


Stream live output logs from a Job
kubectl logs -f job/<job-name> -n stenc-ns


Stream live logs from a specific Pod
kubectl logs -f <pod-name> -n stenc-ns


See why a Pod is stuck in Pending or crashed
kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n stenc-ns


Open an interactive bash terminal inside a running Pod
kubectl exec -it <pod-name> -n stenc-ns -- bash


Delete a finished or failed Job
kubectl delete job <job-name> -n stenc-ns


List ConfigMaps (uploaded scripts)
kubectl get configmaps -n stenc-ns


List Secrets (S3 & app credentials)
kubectl get secrets -n stenc-ns


Check CPU & RAM usage of running Pods
kubectl top pods -n stenc-ns

title: Manual 2: Getting Started with CESNET Kubernetes (e-INFRA CZ / CERIT-SC)
section: 6. Common Pod Statuses Explained
text:
6. Common Pod Statuses Explained
When you run kubectl get pods -n stenc-ns, look at the STATUS column:

Pending / ContainerCreating: Kubernetes is finding a node with enough free CPU/RAM/GPU and downloading the Docker image. If it stays Pending for >5 minutes, run kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n stenc-ns and look at the bottom Events: section (e.g., all GPUs on the cluster might currently be busy).
Running: Your script is actively executing! Run kubectl logs -f <pod-name> -n stenc-ns to watch its progress.
Completed: Your Job finished with Exit Code 0 (success).
Error / CrashLoopBackOff: Your script threw an exception or syntax error. Run kubectl logs <pod-name> -n stenc-ns to read the R/Python traceback.
OOMKilled: Your script exceeded the memory limit defined in your YAML. Increase resources.limits.memory and re-submit.

title: Manual 1: Accessing and Using CESNET S3 Object Storage
text:
CESNET provides high-capacity, S3-compatible object storage (powered by Ceph) where our group stores raw imagery, microscopy scans, ecological datasets (.csv, .rds), and trained deep-learning models.
Because S3 is an object storage system (accessible over HTTPS rather than a traditional local hard drive), you can connect to it from any operating system (Windows, macOS, Linux) as well as directly from R, Python, and Kubernetes Pods.

title: Manual 1: Accessing and Using CESNET S3 Object Storage
section: 1. Connection Details & Credentials
text:
1. Connection Details & Credentials
To connect to our group storage with any tool, you need four pieces of information:







Setting
Value




Endpoint URL
https://s3.cl4.du.cesnet.cz (Host: s3.cl4.du.cesnet.cz, Port: 443)


Bucket Name
peg-bucket (Shared group bucket)


Region
Leave blank / empty ("") or us-east-1 if a tool requires a dummy string


Addressing Style
Path-style (https://s3.cl4.du.cesnet.cz/peg-bucket/...)


Access Key & Secret Key
Obtain from Jakub / the group password manager (or retrieve from Kubernetes if you already have cluster access—see tip below)









Note



Legacy Bucket Note: Older projects prior to migration used endpoint https://s3-old.cl4.du.cesnet.cz with bucket name bucket. All active and new work should use https://s3.cl4.du.cesnet.cz and peg-bucket.



Tip: Retrieving the Group S3 Keys via kubectl
If you already have kubectl configured for our Kubernetes namespace (stenc-ns), you can print the shared S3 Access Key and Secret Key directly in your terminal:
# Print Access Key:
kubectl get secret s3-credentials -n stenc-ns -o jsonpath='{.data.access-key}' | base64 -d ; echo

# Print Secret Key:
kubectl get secret s3-credentials -n stenc-ns -o jsonpath='{.data.secret-key}' | base64 -d ; echo

title: Manual 1: Accessing and Using CESNET S3 Object Storage
section: 2. Which Method Should I Use?
text:
2. Which Method Should I Use?
Choose the workflow that best matches your task:

Method A: Graphical App (Cyberduck or WinSCP) — Best for Windows & macOS users who want to browse folders and drag-and-drop files without using the terminal.
Method B: Mount as a Local Folder (s3fs) — Best for Linux/macOS users who want peg-bucket to appear as a regular directory (~/cesnet_s3) to inspect files or open small tables. (Do not use s3fs for copying 10,000+ small files—use rclone instead!)
Method C: Fast Bulk Transfers & Backups (rclone / aws-cli) — Best when uploading or downloading gigabytes of images, microscopy .czi scans, or .zip datasets. Runs 10x–50x faster than s3fs using parallel threads.
Method D: Direct Access in R (aws.s3) or Python (boto3) — Best for reproducible data analysis scripts so your code reads data straight from S3 and writes outputs back without manual file copying.

title: Manual 1: Accessing and Using CESNET S3 Object Storage
section: 3. Method A: Graphical Point-and-Click (Windows / macOS)
text:
3. Method A: Graphical Point-and-Click (Windows / macOS)

Option 1: Cyberduck (Windows & macOS — Recommended)

Download and install Cyberduck (free and open-source).
Click Open Connection (top-left) and select Amazon S3 from the top dropdown menu.
Fill in the connection dialog:

Server: s3.cl4.du.cesnet.cz
Port: 443
Access Key ID: <YOUR_ACCESS_KEY>
Secret Access Key: <YOUR_SECRET_KEY>

Click More Options (at the bottom of the dialog) and set:

Path: peg-bucket (entering peg-bucket directly here takes you straight into our bucket even if your key does not have permission to list all buckets on the server!)

Click Connect. You can now browse folders, drag-and-drop files to upload/download, and bookmark the connection for one-click access.



Option 2: WinSCP (Windows)

Download and install WinSCP.
In the Login dialog, set:

File protocol: Amazon S3
Host name: s3.cl4.du.cesnet.cz
Port number: 443
Access key ID: <YOUR_ACCESS_KEY>
Secret access key: <YOUR_SECRET_KEY>

Click Advanced… -> Environment -> Directories and set Remote directory to /peg-bucket.
Under Environment -> S3, set URL style to Path (Path-style).
Click OK, then Save the site profile, and click Login.

title: Manual 1: Accessing and Using CESNET S3 Object Storage
section: 4. Method B: Mounting S3 as a Local Folder (s3fs on Linux / macOS)
text:
4. Method B: Mounting S3 as a Local Folder (s3fs on Linux / macOS)
With s3fs, you can mount peg-bucket as a folder in your home directory (e.g., ~/cesnet_s3).

Step 1: Install s3fs

Ubuntu / Debian / Linux Mint:
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y s3fs
Fedora:
sudo dnf install -y s3fs-fuse
macOS (via Homebrew):
brew install --cask macfuse
brew install gromgit/fuse/s3fs-mac



Step 2: Save Your Credentials to ~/.passwd-s3fs
Run the following two commands in your terminal (replace <YOUR_ACCESS_KEY> and <YOUR_SECRET_KEY> with the actual keys; notice the colon : between them and no newline):
printf '<YOUR_ACCESS_KEY>:<YOUR_SECRET_KEY>' > ~/.passwd-s3fs
chmod 600 ~/.passwd-s3fs






Important



s3fs will refuse to run if ~/.passwd-s3fs is readable by other users. chmod 600 ~/.passwd-s3fs is mandatory.




Step 3: Mount the Bucket
You can use our ready-made helper script templates/s3/mount_cesnet_s3.sh, or run the mount command directly:
mkdir -p ~/cesnet_s3
s3fs peg-bucket ~/cesnet_s3 \
  -o passwd_file=${HOME}/.passwd-s3fs \
  -o url=https://s3.cl4.du.cesnet.cz \
  -o use_path_request_style \
  -o uid=$(id -u) \
  -o gid=$(id -g)
Verify that your files are visible:
ls -la ~/cesnet_s3


Step 4: Unmounting (and Fixing “Transport endpoint is not connected”)
When you are done, or if your laptop wakes up from sleep after a Wi-Fi disconnect and ~/cesnet_s3 freezes:
fusermount -u ~/cesnet_s3
# Or if busy/hung:
fusermount -uz ~/cesnet_s3
Then run the s3fs mount command again.

title: Manual 1: Accessing and Using CESNET S3 Object Storage
section: 5. Method C: Fast Bulk Transfers & Backups (rclone & aws-cli)
text:
5. Method C: Fast Bulk Transfers & Backups (rclone & aws-cli)






Tip



Why not use s3fs for large transfers? FUSE mounts (s3fs) process files one-by-one and make multiple metadata calls per file. If you are uploading 5,000 pollinator images or a 20 GB dataset, rclone is 10x to 50x faster because it transfers 16–32 files in parallel and verifies checksums automatically.



Setting up rclone (One-Time Setup)

Install rclone:

Linux: sudo apt install -y rclone
macOS: brew install rclone
Windows: winget install Rclone.Rclone (or download from rclone.org)

Create the configuration file (~/.config/rclone/rclone.conf): Run mkdir -p ~/.config/rclone and add the following block to ~/.config/rclone/rclone.conf:
[cesnet-s3]
type = s3
provider = Ceph
access_key_id = <YOUR_ACCESS_KEY>
secret_access_key = <YOUR_SECRET_KEY>
endpoint = https://s3.cl4.du.cesnet.cz
acl = private



Everyday rclone Commands
# 1. List top-level folders inside peg-bucket
rclone lsd cesnet-s3:peg-bucket

# 2. List directories inside Ostatni/
rclone lsd cesnet-s3:peg-bucket/Ostatni/

# 3. Copy a local folder TO CESNET S3 (High-speed parallel upload)
rclone copy ~/MyProjectData/ cesnet-s3:peg-bucket/Ostatni/MyProjectData/ \
  --update --transfers 16 --checkers 16 --fast-list --progress

# 4. Download a folder FROM CESNET S3 to your computer
rclone copy cesnet-s3:peg-bucket/Ostatni/MyProjectData/ ~/MyProjectData/ \
  --update --transfers 16 --checkers 16 --fast-list --progress






Warning



CRITICAL SAFETY RULE: Always use rclone copy, NOT rclone sync!

rclone copy only adds new or updated files to the destination—it never deletes files on S3.
rclone sync makes the destination identical to the source, meaning if you accidentally point an empty local folder at peg-bucket, rclone sync would delete files from S3! Always use rclone copy (or test first with --dry-run).



See templates/s3/rclone_backup_template.sh for a complete automated backup script with logging.


Using aws-cli (Alternative CLI)
If you prefer the standard Amazon S3 CLI (pip install awscli), always pass --endpoint-url https://s3.cl4.du.cesnet.cz:
export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID="<YOUR_ACCESS_KEY>"
export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY="<YOUR_SECRET_KEY>"

# List contents of peg-bucket
aws --endpoint-url https://s3.cl4.du.cesnet.cz s3 ls s3://peg-bucket/Ostatni/

# Copy a single file to S3
aws --endpoint-url https://s3.cl4.du.cesnet.cz s3 cp results.csv s3://peg-bucket/Ostatni/MyProject/results.csv

# Sync a folder
aws --endpoint-url https://s3.cl4.du.cesnet.cz s3 sync ./my_plots/ s3://peg-bucket/Ostatni/MyProject/my_plots/

title: Manual 1: Accessing and Using CESNET S3 Object Storage
section: 6. Method D: Reading & Writing Directly from R and Python
text:
6. Method D: Reading & Writing Directly from R and Python
Writing scripts that read and write directly to S3 makes your code work identically on your laptop and inside a CESNET Kubernetes Job.

Using CESNET S3 in R (aws.s3)

Store your credentials in ~/.Renviron so you never hardcode keys inside .R scripts: In R, run usethis::edit_r_environ() (or open ~/.Renviron in any text editor) and add:
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID="YOUR_ACCESS_KEY"
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY="YOUR_SECRET_KEY"
AWS_S3_ENDPOINT="s3.cl4.du.cesnet.cz"
AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=""
Restart R after saving ~/.Renviron.
Use aws.s3 in your R script (full template at templates/s3/s3_example.R):
library(aws.s3)

# IMPORTANT: Always set region = "" and base_url = "s3.cl4.du.cesnet.cz"
# Otherwise aws.s3 tries to connect to Amazon's us-east-1 servers!
S3_BUCKET <- "peg-bucket"
S3_HOST   <- "s3.cl4.du.cesnet.cz"

# 1. List files in a folder
files_df <- get_bucket_df(
  bucket = S3_BUCKET,
  prefix = "Ostatni/",
  base_url = S3_HOST,
  region = "",
  use_https = TRUE
)
head(files_df[, c("Key", "Size", "LastModified")])

# 2. Read an .rds file directly from S3 into R memory
my_data <- s3readRDS(
  object = "Ostatni/MyProject/cleaned_data.rds",
  bucket = S3_BUCKET,
  base_url = S3_HOST,
  region = "",
  use_https = TRUE
)

# 3. Save an R object directly to S3 as an .rds file
s3saveRDS(
  x = my_data,
  object = "Ostatni/MyProject/model_output.rds",
  bucket = S3_BUCKET,
  base_url = S3_HOST,
  region = "",
  use_https = TRUE
)

# 4. Upload any local file (e.g. PDF plot or CSV) to S3
put_object(
  file = "figure1.pdf",
  object = "Ostatni/MyProject/figures/figure1.pdf",
  bucket = S3_BUCKET,
  base_url = S3_HOST,
  region = "",
  use_https = TRUE
)



Using CESNET S3 in Python (boto3)
Install boto3 (pip install boto3 pandas) and use the helper pattern below (full template at templates/s3/s3_example.py):
import io
import os
import boto3
from botocore.config import Config
import pandas as pd

S3_ENDPOINT = os.environ.get("S3_ENDPOINT", "https://s3.cl4.du.cesnet.cz")
S3_BUCKET   = os.environ.get("S3_BUCKET", "peg-bucket")

s3 = boto3.client(
    "s3",
    endpoint_url=S3_ENDPOINT,
    aws_access_key_id=os.environ["AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID"],
    aws_secret_access_key=os.environ["AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY"],
    config=Config(signature_version="s3v4"),
)

# 1. Read a CSV directly from S3 into a pandas DataFrame
obj = s3.get_object(Bucket=S3_BUCKET, Key="Ostatni/MyProject/data.csv")
df = pd.read_csv(io.BytesIO(obj["Body"].read()))

# 2. Download a file (e.g. a .zip dataset or .pt model weights)
s3.download_file(S3_BUCKET, "Ostatni/MyProject/dataset.zip", "dataset.zip")

# 3. Upload a local file to S3
s3.upload_file("results.csv", S3_BUCKET, "Ostatni/MyProject/results.csv")

title: Manual 1: Accessing and Using CESNET S3 Object Storage
section: 7. House Rules for peg-bucket Organization
text:
7. House Rules for peg-bucket Organization
To keep our shared bucket clean and easy to navigate for everyone:

Project Folders: Place project-specific datasets under Ostatni/<ProjectName>/ (e.g., Ostatni/Stomata/, Ostatni/Pollen_viability/, Ostatni/YOLO_flies/, Ostatni/RhizoPic/) or your dedicated top-level project directory.
Avoid Millions of Tiny Loose Files: When uploading training datasets with >10,000 small cropped images for Kubernetes GPU jobs, pack them into a single .zip or .tar file in a staged_area/ subfolder too. Downloading a single 2 GB .zip file inside a Kubernetes Job takes 5 seconds; downloading 20,000 tiny .jpg files individually takes 15 minutes!
Never Run rclone sync or aws s3 rm --recursive Without Checking Path Twice: Double-check your target prefix before deleting or overwriting data.

title: Manual 3: Running R and Python Scripts on CESNET Kubernetes
text:
One of the biggest misconceptions about Kubernetes is that you must build and push a new Docker image every time you edit a line of R or Python code.
In our group’s workflow, you do NOT need to build Docker images for 95% of scripts. Instead, we use:

title: Manual 3: Running R and Python Scripts on CESNET Kubernetes
section: 1. The Fastest Way: One-Command Launcher (run_script_on_k8s.sh)
text:
1. The Fastest Way: One-Command Launcher (run_script_on_k8s.sh)
If you already have an .R or .py script that reads its inputs from CESNET S3 and writes its outputs back to CESNET S3, you can run it on the cluster with a single terminal command using templates/k8s/run_script_on_k8s.sh:
# Run an R script on 8 CPU cores & 16 GB RAM (default):
./templates/k8s/run_script_on_k8s.sh my_analysis.R

# Run a heavy R script requesting 16 CPU cores & 32 GB RAM:
./templates/k8s/run_script_on_k8s.sh heavy_simulation.R --cpu 16 --mem 32Gi

# Run a Python script on an NVIDIA GPU:
./templates/k8s/run_script_on_k8s.sh train_yolo.py --gpu
What run_script_on_k8s.sh does behind the scenes:

Packages your local .R or .py file into a Kubernetes ConfigMap.
Creates a CERIT-SC security-compliant Job with s3-credentials environment variables (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, S3_ENDPOINT, S3_BUCKET=peg-bucket).
Waits for the pod to start and streams the live output logs to your terminal. (Note: Pressing Ctrl+C only stops log streaming on your laptop—the job keeps running on the cluster!)

title: Manual 3: Running R and Python Scripts on CESNET Kubernetes
section: 2. Step-by-Step: Running an R Script on Kubernetes (r-cpu-job.yaml)
text:
2. Step-by-Step: Running an R Script on Kubernetes (r-cpu-job.yaml)
If you want full control over R packages or multi-file scripts, follow this 3-step workflow using templates/k8s/r-cpu-job.yaml.

Step 1: Write Your R Script (my_analysis.R)
Because the Kubernetes pod starts with an empty local disk (/app/workspace), your R script should read input files from peg-bucket and upload output files back to peg-bucket:
# my_analysis.R
library(aws.s3)

S3_BUCKET <- Sys.getenv("S3_BUCKET", unset = "peg-bucket")
S3_HOST   <- "s3.cl4.du.cesnet.cz"

cat("1. Downloading input dataset from CESNET S3...\n")
save_object(
  object   = "Ostatni/MyProject/input_data.csv",
  bucket   = S3_BUCKET,
  file     = "input_data.csv",
  base_url = S3_HOST,
  region   = "",
  use_https = TRUE
)

df <- read.csv("input_data.csv")
cat("Loaded", nrow(df), "rows.\n")

# --- Run your statistical model / simulation here ---
summary_df <- aggregate(. ~ site, data = df, FUN = mean)
write.csv(summary_df, "summary_results.csv", row.names = FALSE)
saveRDS(summary_df, "summary_results.rds")

cat("2. Uploading results back to CESNET S3...\n")
put_object(
  file     = "summary_results.csv",
  object   = "Ostatni/MyProject/outputs/summary_results.csv",
  bucket   = S3_BUCKET,
  base_url = S3_HOST,
  region   = "",
  use_https = TRUE
)
put_object(
  file     = "summary_results.rds",
  object   = "Ostatni/MyProject/outputs/summary_results.rds",
  bucket   = S3_BUCKET,
  base_url = S3_HOST,
  region   = "",
  use_https = TRUE
)
cat("All done!\n")


Step 2: Upload the Script as a ConfigMap
Run this command in your terminal whenever you create or update my_analysis.R:
kubectl create configmap my-r-script -n stenc-ns \
  --from-file=my_analysis.R=my_analysis.R \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
(You can also pass multiple --from-file= arguments if your R script calls source("helper_functions.R")!)


Step 3: Submit the Job & Watch the Logs
Copy templates/k8s/r-cpu-job.yaml to your project directory, adjust the list of CRAN packages (pkgs <- c("aws.s3", "lme4", "brms", ...)) or CPU/RAM limits if needed, and submit:
# Delete any old finished job with the same name first:
kubectl delete job r-analysis-job -n stenc-ns --ignore-not-found

# Start the job:
kubectl apply -f r-cpu-job.yaml

# Watch live R output:
kubectl logs -f job/r-analysis-job -n stenc-ns






Note



How R Package Installation Works in Non-Root Pods: Because CERIT-SC pods run as user 1000, R cannot write to /usr/local/lib/R/site-library. In templates/k8s/r-cpu-job.yaml, we set R_LIBS_USER=/app/R_libs (on the writable /app volume) so install.packages() works without root permissions!

title: Manual 3: Running R and Python Scripts on CESNET Kubernetes
section: 3. Step-by-Step: Running a Python Script on CPU (python-cpu-job.yaml)
text:
3. Step-by-Step: Running a Python Script on CPU (python-cpu-job.yaml)

Step 1: Write Your Python Script (process_data.py)
# process_data.py
import os
import boto3
from botocore.config import Config
import pandas as pd

S3_ENDPOINT = os.environ["S3_ENDPOINT"]
S3_BUCKET   = os.environ["S3_BUCKET"]

s3 = boto3.client(
    "s3",
    endpoint_url=S3_ENDPOINT,
    aws_access_key_id=os.environ["AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID"],
    aws_secret_access_key=os.environ["AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY"],
    config=Config(signature_version="s3v4"),
)

print("1. Downloading input data from S3...")
s3.download_file(S3_BUCKET, "Ostatni/MyProject/raw_counts.csv", "raw_counts.csv")

df = pd.read_csv("raw_counts.csv")
print(f"Processing {len(df)} records...")

# --- Your computation here ---
df["normalized"] = df["count"] / df["count"].sum()
df.to_csv("processed_counts.csv", index=False)

print("2. Uploading results to S3...")
s3.upload_file("processed_counts.csv", S3_BUCKET, "Ostatni/MyProject/processed_counts.csv")
print("Done!")


Step 2: Upload the ConfigMap and Submit templates/k8s/python-cpu-job.yaml
# 1. Upload/update your Python script ConfigMap
kubectl create configmap my-python-script -n stenc-ns \
  --from-file=process_data.py=process_data.py \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -

# 2. Submit the Job
kubectl delete job python-cpu-job -n stenc-ns --ignore-not-found
kubectl apply -f templates/k8s/python-cpu-job.yaml

# 3. Follow live logs
kubectl logs -f job/python-cpu-job -n stenc-ns

title: Manual 3: Running R and Python Scripts on CESNET Kubernetes
section: 4. Step-by-Step: Running a GPU Job (YOLO / PyTorch Deep Learning)
text:
4. Step-by-Step: Running a GPU Job (YOLO / PyTorch Deep Learning)
When training computer vision models (e.g., YOLO pollen detection, hoverfly tracking, stomata segmentation, root segmentation), use templates/k8s/python-gpu-job.yaml.

Three Golden Rules for GPU Jobs on CERIT-SC:

Always Mount /dev/shm (Shared Memory): By default, Kubernetes gives containers only 64 MB of /dev/shm. PyTorch and Ultralytics YOLO DataLoader workers use /dev/shm to pass image batches between CPU and GPU; with only 64 MB, your training job will crash mid-epoch with RuntimeError: DataLoader worker (pid ...) is killed by signal: Bus error. Our template templates/k8s/python-gpu-job.yaml mounts a 4 GiB RAM-backed /dev/shm volume:
     volumeMounts:
     - name: dshm
       mountPath: /dev/shm
   volumes:
   - name: dshm
     emptyDir:
       medium: Memory
       sizeLimit: 4Gi
Stage Training Datasets as a Single .zip on S3 and Unpack into /app/workspace: Never train a model directly over an s3fs mount! Instead, pack your training images and labels into a .zip archive on S3 (s3://peg-bucket/Ostatni/MyProject/dataset.zip), download it into /app/workspace at the start of the job using aws s3 cp, unzip it locally on the fast node SSD, run training, and aws s3 sync the runs/ folder back to peg-bucket when finished.
Set Writable Config Directories for Non-Root User 1000: Tools like Ultralytics YOLO and Matplotlib try to write config files to ~/.config. Always export:
export HOME=/app
export YOLO_CONFIG_DIR=/app/.config/Ultralytics



Submitting a GPU Job
# 1. Upload your training script to the ConfigMap
kubectl create configmap my-gpu-script -n stenc-ns \
  --from-file=train.py=train.py \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -

# 2. Submit the GPU job
kubectl delete job python-gpu-job -n stenc-ns --ignore-not-found
kubectl apply -f templates/k8s/python-gpu-job.yaml

# 3. Monitor training epochs live
kubectl logs -f job/python-gpu-job -n stenc-ns

section: 6. Housekeeping: Cleaning Up Finished Jobs
text:
6. Housekeeping: Cleaning Up Finished Jobs
Completed jobs (STATUS: Completed) do not use CPU or GPU, but keeping dozens of old failed/completed jobs clutters kubectl get pods. Once you have verified your outputs are safely in peg-bucket:
# Delete a specific job (this also deletes its pod and logs):
kubectl delete job <job-name> -n stenc-ns

# Delete all successfully completed jobs in stenc-ns at once:
kubectl delete jobs --field-selector status.successful=1 -n stenc-ns
